style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly. Transliterations are ASCII-normalized (lowercase, diacritics dropped) relative to the lexicon's spellings.
chapterNote: Chapter 9 is the grand finale of the book's prologue (chs. 1-9), and it is built as a deliberate diptych: two women, two houses, two banquets, two invitations -- worded almost identically so the contrast is unmistakable. Lady Wisdom builds her house on seven pillars, slaughters her feast, and sends her maidens to cry the same call from the heights of the city (vv. 1-6); Lady Folly sits brazen at her own door and cries that very same line to the very same passers-by (vv. 13-18). Between them stands a hinge of sayings on who can be taught (vv. 7-12), anchored by the book's master text restated: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (v. 10). The simple young man must choose which table to come to -- one leads to life and understanding, the other to guests already in the depths of Sheol.

1.text: Her house Wisdom has raised up, quarrying out its seven pillars from the rock.
1.amp: Wisdom [chokmot -- Wisdom in the grand plural, personified as a great lady] has built [banah -- constructed and established] her house [bayith], she has hewn out [chatsab -- quarried and cut from stone] her seven pillars [ammud];
1.notes: chokmot (H2454) is the majestic plural of chokmah -- Wisdom portrayed as a noble woman of substance who builds (banah, H1129) a real house. The seven pillars (sheba', H7651) suggest a house of completeness and permanence, fit for a feast; the number of fullness for a structure meant to stand. Also tagged: bayith (H1004), chatsab (H2672), ammud (H5982).

2.text: She has slaughtered her beasts, she has mixed her wine, she has also spread her table.
2.amp: She has slaughtered [tabach -- butchered for a feast] her beasts, she has mixed [masak -- blended wine with spice, the festal preparation] her wine [yayin], she has also arranged [arak -- set in good order] her table [shulchan];
2.notes: Wisdom prepares a lavish banquet: tabach (H2873) is to slaughter for a meal, masak (H4537) is to mix wine with spices for celebration, and arak (H6186) is to set out in proper order -- the same verb used for arraying troops or laying out an altar. Everything is ready before the guests are even called. Also tagged: yayin (H3196), shulchan (H7979).

3.text: She has sent out her maidens; she calls aloud from the highest places of the city:
3.amp: She has sent out [shalach -- dispatched as heralds] her maidens [naarah -- her young servant-girls], she cries [qara -- proclaims aloud] from the heights [marom -- the loftiest, most public points] of the city;
3.notes: Wisdom does not whisper in corners; she sends her maidens (naarah, H5291) as public heralds and herself proclaims (qara, H7121) from the marom (H4791), the highest and most visible places. Her invitation is open, witnessed, and free -- the deliberate opposite of Folly's furtive appeal in v. 17. Also tagged: shalach (H7971).

4.text: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To the one who lacks heart she says,
4.amp: "Whoever is simple [peti -- the naive, the easily-swayed], let him turn in [sur -- turn aside off the road] here!" To him that lacks [chaser] heart [leb -- understanding, the seat of judgment] she says [amar],
4.notes: the peti (H6612) is the open, undecided young man -- not yet hardened, still able to be won. To 'lack heart' (chaser leb, H2638 + H3820) is to lack judgment, since in Hebrew the leb is the seat of thought and will, not mere feeling. Wisdom's call targets exactly the one Folly will target with the identical words in v. 16. Also tagged: sur (H5493), amar (H559).

5.text: "Turn this way and feed on what I have set before you; taste the wine I blended for you.
5.amp: "Come [yalak -- come and walk this way], eat [lacham -- partake, feed] of my bread [lechem], and drink [shatah] of the wine [yayin] which I have mixed [masak];
5.notes: to eat Wisdom's bread (lechem, H3899) and drink her mixed wine (yayin, H3196) is to take her instruction into oneself as nourishment -- the feast is the teaching. The same prepared wine of v. 2 is now offered freely; what she labored to set out, she gives away (cf. Isa 55:1-2). Also tagged: yalak (H3212), lacham (H3898 -- a root spanning both 'to feed on' and 'to do battle'; here, to eat), shatah (H8354), masak (H4537).

6.text: Forsake the foolish, and live; and walk straight in the way of understanding."
6.amp: Forsake [azab -- abandon, leave behind] the foolish [petaim -- the simple ways, the naivety itself], and live [chayah -- truly live, find life]; and go straight [ashar -- advance, go straight on] in the way [derek] of understanding [binah]."
6.notes: the call is two-sided: azab (H5800), forsake the old simplicity, and chayah (H2421), live -- not bare survival but the full life wisdom gives. ashar (H833) carries the sense of going straight ahead and of being made happy or blessed; the way of binah (H998) is both the right road and the road that leads to flourishing. Also tagged: petaim (H6612, plural of peti), derek (H1870).

7.text: He who corrects a scoffer brings shame on himself, and he who rebukes a wicked man gets himself a stain.
7.amp: He that reproves [yasar -- instructs by correction] a scoffer [luts -- the mocker who sneers at correction] takes for himself shame [qalon -- disgrace, dishonor], and he that rebukes [yakach -- reproves, sets right] a wicked man [rasha] gets himself a blemish [mum];
7.notes: the hinge-section opens with hard realism: yasar (H3256) and yakach (H3198) are honest correction, but aimed at the luts (H3887), the entrenched scoffer, they boomerang into qalon (H7036) and mum (H3971) for the one offering them. Not all are teachable; wisdom knows when correction will only draw abuse. Also tagged: rasha (H7563).

8.text: Do not rebuke a scoffer, or he will hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.
8.amp: Reprove [yakach] not a scoffer [luts], lest he hate [sane] you; rebuke [yakach] a wise man [chakham], and he will love [ahab] you;
8.notes: the same verb yakach (H3198) yields opposite fruit depending on the heart that receives it: the luts (H3887) repays correction with sane (H8130), hatred, while the chakham (H2450), the wise, repays the very same rebuke with ahab (H157), love. A man's response to correction reveals which one he is.

9.text: Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be wiser still; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.
9.amp: Give [natan] to a wise man [chakham], and he will be yet wiser [chakam -- grow wise, gain in wisdom]; make known [yada -- teach, cause to know] to a just man [tsaddiq], and he will increase [yasaph -- add, multiply] in learning [leqach];
9.notes: wisdom is self-multiplying in the teachable: give to the chakham (H2450) and he becomes wiser (chakam, H2449); teach the tsaddiq (H6662) and he adds (yasaph, H3254) to his leqach (H3948), what he has taken in. The wise are not finished -- they are precisely the ones who keep growing (cf. Prov 1:5). Also tagged: natan (H5414), yada (H3045).

10.text: Where wisdom starts is in the reverent fear of the LORD; to know the Holy One -- that is what understanding means.
10.amp: The fear [yirah -- reverent awe] of the LORD [YHWH] is the beginning [techillah -- the starting-point and first principle] of wisdom [chokmah], and the knowledge [daat] of the Holy One [qadosh] is understanding [binah];
10.notes: the book's master text, restated at its prologue's climax (cf. 1:7): yirat YHWH (H3374 + H3068) is the techillah (H8462), the very first thing, of chokmah (H2451). To know the qadosh (H6918), the Holy One -- the plural-of-majesty for God -- is itself binah (H998). Wisdom is not first technique but relationship: it begins where a man bows before the holy God. Also tagged: daat (H1847).

11.text: Through me your days grow many, and to the span of your life still more years are joined.
11.amp: For by me your days [yom] shall be multiplied [rabah -- become many, increase], and the years [shanah] of your life [chay] shall be increased [yasaph -- added to];
11.notes: Wisdom speaks in the first person again (as in 8:35): rabah (H7235) and yasaph (H3254) promise lengthened days and added years -- not a magic charm but the natural fruit of a life ordered by wisdom and the fear of God, which keeps a man from the self-destroying paths that cut life short (cf. 3:2; 10:27). Also tagged: yom (H3117), shanah (H8141), chay (H2416).

12.text: If you are wise, you are wise for your own good; but if you scoff, you alone will bear it.
12.amp: If you be wise [chakam], you are wise for yourself; but if you scorn [luts -- play the mocker], you alone shall bear [nasa -- carry, lift the weight of] it;
12.notes: wisdom and folly are finally personal accounts: to be wise (chakam, H2449) profits the man himself, and to scoff (luts, H3887) is a weight he alone must nasa (H5375) -- carry. No one is wise or foolish by proxy; each bears the harvest of his own choosing (cf. Gal 6:5). The hinge-section closes, and the second woman now rises to her door.

13.text: The woman of folly is loud; she is naive and knows nothing at all.
13.amp: A foolish [kesilut -- the loud-mouthed stupidity that is Folly personified] woman [ishshah] is clamorous [hamah -- turbulent, roaring, restless]; she is simple [petiyut], and knows [yada] nothing [bal -- not, never a thing];
13.notes: Folly is unveiled as Wisdom's dark mirror: where Wisdom (chokmot) is dignified and composed, this ishshah kesilut (H802 + H3687) is hamah (H1993) -- loud, unsettled, all noise. She is herself simple (petiyut, H6615) and knows nothing (yada... bal, H3045 + H1077); she cannot give what she does not possess.

14.text: She sits at the door of her house, on a seat in the high places of the city,
14.amp: For she sits [yashab -- is settled, takes her place] at the door [petach -- the opening, the entrance] of her house [bayith], on a seat [kisse -- a chair, a throne] in the high places [marom] of the city;
14.notes: Folly mimics Wisdom's posture point for point: she too claims the marom (H4791), the high places of v. 3, but where Wisdom sent maidens out into the streets, Folly merely sits (yashab, H3427) enthroned (kisse, H3678) at her own petach (H6607), the doorway, advertising herself rather than serving a feast. Also tagged: bayith (H1004).

15.text: to call out to those who pass by, who go straight on their ways:
15.amp: To call [qara -- to hail, to summon] to those who pass by [abar -- cross over, travel through] on the way [derek], who go right [yashar -- straight, upright] on their paths [orach];
15.notes: her target is the same as Wisdom's, and chosen with cruel precision: travelers who 'go right' (yashar, H3474) on their orach (H734), people currently walking the straight road. Folly does not hunt the already-fallen; she calls out to those still keeping the path, trying to pull them off it (qara, H7121 -- the same verb as Wisdom's cry in v. 3). Also tagged: abar (H5674), derek (H1870).

16.text: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to the one who lacks heart she says,
16.amp: "Whoever is simple [peti], let him turn in [sur] here!" And to him that lacks [chaser] heart [leb] she says [amar],
16.notes: Folly's invitation is word-for-word Wisdom's in v. 4 -- the same peti (H6612), the same 'turn in,' the same 'lacks heart' (chaser leb, H2638 + H3820). The two voices sound identical at the door; the difference is hidden entirely in what waits inside. This is the chapter's whole point: the call is the same, the destination is death or life. Also tagged: sur (H5493), amar (H559).

17.text: "Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."
17.amp: "Stolen [ganab -- thieved, taken by stealth] waters are sweet [mathaq -- proven sweet, made sweet], and bread [lechem] eaten in secret [sether -- hiddenness, concealment] is pleasant [naem -- delightful, agreeable]."
17.notes: here the two feasts diverge utterly. Wisdom's bread was prepared, mixed, and freely given (vv. 2, 5); Folly's appeal is precisely that her bread is stolen (ganab, H1589) and her pleasure secret (sether, H5643). The whole lure is the forbidden thrill of the illicit -- the very sweetness lies in the theft and the concealment (cf. 5:15-18, where lawful waters are commended instead). Also tagged: mathaq (H4985), lechem (H3899), naem (H5276).

18.text: Yet it escapes him that the dead lie within those walls -- that everyone she has invited has sunk to the deepest reaches of Sheol.
18.amp: But he knows [yada] not that the dead [rephaim -- the shades, the lifeless spirits of the departed] are there; that her guests [qara -- her invited ones] are in the depths [ameq -- the unsearchable lowlands] of Sheol [sheol -- the grave, the realm of the dead];
18.notes: the curtain is pulled back on Folly's house: her dining hall is a tomb. The rephaim (H7496), the shades of the dead, fill her rooms, and her guests have already sunk to the ameq (H6012), the depths, of Sheol (H7585). The simple man does not know (yada, H3045) it -- the one thing he most needs to know. The book's prologue ends here, at the two tables: Wisdom's, which leads to life, and Folly's, which opens straight onto the grave. Also tagged: qara (H7121, her 'called ones').
